והנה בפ"ק דמציעא (דף ח') משמע דגם בשניהן רוכבין כל אחד מבטל קנין חבירו אי לאו דמגביה מציאה לחבירו ע"ש בש"ס דרצו להוכיח דמגביה מציאה לחבירו קנה חבירו מהא דתנן זה אומר כולי שלי וז"א חציו שלי הא תו למה לי ש"מ ממשנה יתירה המגביה מציא' לחבירו קנה חבירו ופרש"י ומשום הכי יחלוקו דאמרינן שניהם הגביהו וה"ל כל אחד מגביה מציאה לו ולחבירו דאי משום דלא ידעינן הי מינייהו משקר הא מרישא שמעינן וע"ש דדחי לה עד דמייתי אלא מהא שנים רוכבין ע"ג בהמה הא תו למה לי אלא ממשנה יתירה ש"מ המגביה מציאה לחבירו כו' משמע דגבי שניהם רוכבין נמי צריך למגביה מציאה לחבירו ואי לאו דמגביה מציאה לחבירו קונה חבירו קנין אחד מבטל קנין חבירו ולא קנו שניהם וא"כ חרש ופקח דלא שייך מגביה מציאה לחבירו לא קנה כלל:

אמנם בשטה מקובצת שם כת' בשם הריטב"א בהא דמייתי משניהם רוכבין היינו דמייתי ממשנה יתירה דקמ"ל דכי היכא דבשניהם רוכבין החלוקה היא מצד שקנו שניהם יחד ברכיבה ה"נ בריש' בשנים אוחזין בטלית החלוקה הוא מצד שקנו שניהם יחד בהגבהה ע' שם ומשמע דברכיבה קנו שניהם אפילו בלא טעמא דמגביה מציאה לחבירו ומשום דקנין דאזיל מחמתי' לא מבטל א' קנין חבירו וא"כ בחרש ופקח שרכבו יחד או הנהיגו קנה פקח כולו אבל מדברי רש"י שם נראה דגם ברכיבה מצד מגביה מציאה לחבירו היא ע"ש (דף ח') וברש"י פ"ק דמציעא (דף ט') ד"ה אלא רכוב במקום מנהיג וז"ל שניהם באים לפנינו זה רכוב וזה מנהיג ז"א כולה שלי וזה אמר כולה שלי אמר שמואל חד קני ע"ש ונראה מלשון רש"י דלענין קנין לא מספקא ליה הי מינייהו עדיף אלא לענין מוחזקין מספקא ליה הי מינייהו עדיף אלא לענין מוחזקין מספקא ליה מי מיקרי מוחזק טפי אי רכוב אי מנהיג אבל בתוס' שם כתבו דלענין מוחזקין ודאי שניהם שוין ולא מספקא אלא לענין קנין הי מינייהו עדיף. ונרא' דרש"י דס"ל דגבי שניהם רוכבין נמי מבטל אחד קנין חבירו אי לאו משום מגביה מציאה לחבירו וכיון דהתם מספקא ליה רכוב עדיף משום דתפיס במוסירה ודאי מוסירה לא קנה אלא דקנין רכוב משום אזלי' מחמתי' ומספקא ליה משום דרכוב תפיס במוסירה משוה ליה להיות עדיף ממנהיג וכיון דנרא' דעת רש"י דבשניהן רוכבין נמי מבטל א' קנין חבירו וא"כ היכי מצינו למימר דדכוב עדיף לקנין משום תפוס במוסירה דהא מוסירה אינו קונה ואינו אלא מצד אזלא מחמתי' ומנהיג דהוי נמי אזל' מחמתי' משוי ליה המוסירה להיות עדיף וע"ש בתוספות והא קנין דאזלא מחמתי' דרכוב לאו כלום הוא כיון דאזלא נמי מחמתי' דמנהיג ומבטל א' קנין חבירו ומשום מגביה מציאה לחבירו לא שייך כיון דאמרת מנהיג לא קנה וה"ל כמו חרש ופקח דלא זכו תרוייהו כיון דחרש מבטל קנין הפקח וה"נ מבטל המנהיג קנין דאזיל מחמתי' דרכוב ומשום תפיס במוסירה לחודיה אינו קונה. להכי כת' רש"י לפרש משום מוחזקין הוא דמספקא ליה מי עדיף אבל לקנין ע"כ שניהן שוין דאי אמרת רכוב קנה ומנהיג לא קנה א"כ רכוב נמי לא קנה וכמ"ש: ותוס' דמפרשי לה לענין קנין נרא' דסברי כשיטת הריטב"א דבשניהן רוכבין א"צ לטעמי' דמגביה מציאה לחבירו ומשום דאזיל מחמתי' אילו מבטל א' קנין חבירו וא"כ שפיר מצינו למימר דרכוב קונה ומנהיג לא קנה וקנין דרכוב משום דאזלא מחמתי' ועדיפותא דידיה משום תפוס במוסירה ומנהיג לא מבטל את אזלא מחמתי' דרכוב. ובזה ניחא לשון רש"י פ"ק דמציעא (דף ח') ד"ה ש"מ רכוב קני וז"ל וכיון דשלא במקום מנהיג קנה כו' במקום מנהיג פליגי עכ"ל. וכולם תמהו בדברי רש"י דהא הכי ס"ד בש"ס אמימרא דרכוב קני ואפי' רכוב במקום מנהיג ס"ד דחד מינייהו עדיף וע' בשטה מקובצת שהאריך הרבה ליישב דברי רש"י וע"ש מהרש"א. ולפמ"ש ניחא דרש"י ס"ל דהא דבעי לה רכוב במקום מנהיג היינו לענין מוחזקין בז"א כולה שלי אבל לענין קנין פליגי דליכא למימר דרכוב עדיף דא"כ לא קני כלום במקום מנהיג דכל א' מבטל קנין אזלא מחמתי' דחברי' ומתוך שזה לא קני זה לא קני כדאמרי' גבי חרש ופקח ומש"ה כת' רש"י לענין קנין פליגי ודוק:
en_segments: A deaf-mute and a person of sound mind who lifted it. I was uncertain about a deaf-mute and a competent person who were both riding an animal or leading it. Is this like the case where both lift a found object, so that neither acquires, or does the defect arise only in hagbahah because one person must lift the entire object off the ground? There, when the deaf-mute holds part of it, it is as though half remains on the ground. Riding or leading, however, is an acquisition because the animal moves through his force. Perhaps one participant's ineffective act does not nullify the other's acquisition, and the competent person acquires the whole.

The first chapter of Bava Metzia 8 appears to indicate that even where two people ride, each would nullify the other's acquisition were it not for the rule that one who lifts a found object for another acquires it for the other. The Gemara initially seeks to prove that rule from the Mishnah where one says, 'It is entirely mine,' and the other says, 'Half is mine.' Why is this additional case needed? The redundant Mishnah teaches that one who lifts a found object for his fellow acquires for him. Rashi explains that they divide because we treat both as having lifted the object jointly, so each is lifting for himself and his fellow. If the division rested merely on uncertainty which party lies, the first clause would already teach it. The Gemara rejects that proof and later brings the case of two people riding an animal as the redundant Mishnah teaching the same rule. This implies that even with two riders we need the doctrine that one acquires for his fellow. Without it, each one's acquisition would interfere with the other's and neither would acquire. Therefore, if the pair are a deaf-mute and a competent person, where the doctrine of acquiring for one's fellow cannot operate in the ordinary manner, perhaps neither acquires.

Shitah Mekubetzet, however, cites Ritva explaining that the proof from two riders is only from the redundancy of the case. The Mishnah teaches that just as the two riders divide because they each acquired simultaneously through riding, so too the opening case of two people holding a garment divides because they acquired simultaneously through lifting. This implies that two riders acquire even without the doctrine that one lifts for his fellow. An acquisition based on causing the animal to move does not have one participant nullify the other's act. According to this, where a deaf-mute and a competent person ride or lead together, the competent person acquires the whole.

Rashi appears to hold otherwise, treating two riders as dependent upon the doctrine of acquiring for one's fellow. In Bava Metzia 9, s.v. 'rather, one riding where another leads,' Rashi explains the question as a case where one party rides and one leads, each saying the entire animal is his, and Shmuel says one of them acquires. Rashi's wording suggests that the uncertainty is not which act is legally capable of acquisition in the abstract, but which party is considered the stronger possessor. Tosafos explain the question as one of acquisition itself, asking which mode is stronger.

Rashi's approach is understandable in light of his view that where two people ride, each one's movement-causing acquisition would nullify the other's were it not for the doctrine that one acquires for his fellow. In the rider-versus-leader case, the possibility that riding is superior because the rider also holds the reins cannot mean that the reins independently acquire. The rider's acquisition remains based on the animal's moving through his force, just like the leader's. If the leader's act had no acquisition at all, then according to Rashi the rider's movement-based acquisition would likewise fail in the leader's presence, just as a competent person's acquisition fails when coupled with a deaf-mute whose ineffective participation prevents joint acquisition. The rider cannot be saved through the doctrine of acquiring for his fellow if we say the leader himself acquired nothing. Thus Rashi frames the question as which one has the stronger possession for purposes of adjudicating competing claims, while for pure acquisition both must stand equally. Tosafos, who frame the question as which acquisition is legally stronger, appear to follow Ritva's view that simultaneous riding does not require the doctrine of acquiring for another. An act that causes movement can coexist with another's similar act. It is therefore possible that riding acquires and leading does not, with the rider's acquisition remaining effective even though the leader also caused movement.

This also resolves Rashi's difficult wording on Bava Metzia 8, s.v. 'learn from here that riding acquires': 'Since he acquires when there is no leader, where there is a leader they disagree.' Commentators wondered, because the Gemara originally understood Shmuel's statement to ask whether one mode is stronger even in the presence of the other. According to what I wrote, Rashi means that the dispute concerning acquisition itself can exist only insofar as both modes are otherwise equal. If one said that the rider alone acquires and the leader does not, then according to Rashi the rider would also fail in the leader's presence, because each movement-based act would interfere with the other and the doctrine of acquiring for one's fellow could not rescue the rider when the leader himself has no acquisition. Hence for acquisition they must be treated alike, and the Gemara's question concerns their relative status as possessors. This is precise.

he_segments: הפורש מצוד' בשדה חבירו. כת' הרב המגיד פ"א מזכי' וז"ל לפי שזה שפרס מצוד' בשד' חבירו שלא ברשות לא תיקנו חכמים שיהי' בהם גזל מפני דרכי שלום וכת' תדע לך שהרי אמרו שם דבמצוד' שיש להם הלוקח משם הוא גזלן ואי ברשות חבירו לא קנה ק"ו מכליו של לוקח ברשות מוכר שאע"פ שיש שם דעת אחרת מקנ' דלא קנה אלא ודאי בפורש שלא ברשות אפי' יש למצוד' תוך קנה בעל הקרקע אם היא חצר המשתמר ואם אינו משתמר בעומד תוך שדהו ואמר זכת' לי שדי קנה עכ"ל. וע"פ זה הוא סעיף זה:

ובלחם משנה שם ז"ל ותמיהא לי טובא דכי היכ' דקי"ל כליו של לוקח ברשות מוכר לא קנה לוקח ה"נ קי"ל דכליו של מוכר ברשות לוקח לא קנה לוקח וכדכת' בפ"ז ממכיר' וא"כ כי היכי דהרב המגיד דן ק"ו לשלא יזכ' בעל המצוד' גם כן נדון ק"ו לשלא יזכ' בעל השד' ונא' מה התם דעת אחרת מקנ' אותן לא קני רשותו ללוקח משום דמפסיק כליו של מוכר כאן דליכא דעת אחרת מקנ' אינו דין שלא תקנ' רשותו לבעל השדה כיון דהמצוד' שיש לו תוך שהוא כלי מפסיק וע"ש שהאריך בקושיא והניח בצ"ע:

ולענ"ד נרא' דכליו לא מיקרי אלא היכא שיש לו רשות להניח שם כליו וכדמוכח מתוס' פרק הספינ' דף פ"ה שהקשו מאי קא מבעיא בכליו של לוקח ברשות מוכר הא אמרינן התם דכליו של לוקח ברשות הרבים לכ"ע לא קנה כו' ותירצו דוקא ברשות הרבים משום דמאן שביק ליה אבל בכליו של לוקח ברשות מוכר מספקא ליה דאפשר משאיל לו מקום כי היכא דליקני ברוצ' למכור וע"ש ובטור סי' ר' כת' בשם הרמ"ה דמיירי דהמוכר נתן לו רשות לאנוחי כליו ברשותו אלא כיון דלא א"ל זיל קני בפירוש לא יהיב ליה אדעתי' לאקנויי ע"ש וכה"ג נמי כליו של מוכר ברשות לוקח משום דהמוכר מכניס כליו ללוקח ברשות לוקח מש"ה מספקא להו בש"ס אי קנה לוקח משום שכליו של מוכר המה מפסיקין ומבעיא להו אם מתבטל הכלי אצל הרשות או לא אבל הכא בפורס מצוד' שלא ברשות בעל השד' לא מיקרי כליו להפסק' כלל וקונ' בעל השד' ומה שכת' הרב המגיד לדון ק"ו מכליו של לוקח ברשות מוכר שאע"פ שיש שם דעת אחרת מקנ' בתרתי הוי ק"ו דכליו של לוקח אינו אלא כשהניח ברשות מוכר וגם איכא דעת אחרת מקנ' ומכ"ש פורע שלא ברשות דלא מיקרי כליו כלל גם ליכא דעת אחרת מקנ' אבל בעל השד' שפיר קונ' דלא מיקרי כליו להפסק' כיון שמכניס שם בשד' שלא ברשות לא מפסיק כלל וזה ברור ודו"ק:
en_segments: One who spreads a trap in another person's field. Maggid Mishneh, chapter 1 of Hilchot Zechiyah, explains that one who spreads a trap in another's field without permission was not granted the rabbinic protection against taking what entered the trap, even for the sake of peaceful relations. He proves it from the rule that where the trap has an enclosed receptacle, one who takes from it is a robber. If the trap stood in another person's domain, its owner would not acquire, all the more so than a buyer's vessel in the seller's domain, where even though the seller consciously transfers ownership, the buyer may not acquire. Thus where one spreads a trap without permission, even if the trap has an enclosure, the owner of the land acquires the captured item if the land is a guarded courtyard, or if it is unguarded when he stands there and says, 'My field shall acquire for me.' This is the basis of the present seif.

Lechem Mishneh objects: just as a buyer's vessel in the seller's domain does not acquire for the buyer, we also rule that a seller's vessel in the buyer's domain prevents the buyer from acquiring. If Maggid Mishneh uses an a fortiori argument to deny acquisition to the trap owner, the same a fortiori argument should deny acquisition to the field owner. If the buyer's domain cannot acquire where the seller's vessel intervenes even though another person is consciously transferring ownership, then here, where there is no conscious transferor, all the more so should the landowner's domain fail because the trap, which is the trap owner's vessel, intervenes. Lechem Mishneh leaves this difficult.

In my opinion, an object is called another person's 'vessel' for this purpose only where he has permission to place it there. Tosafos in chapter HaSefinah, Bava Batra 85, ask why the Gemara is uncertain about a buyer's vessel in the seller's domain when it already says that a buyer's vessel in the public domain unquestionably does not acquire. They answer that in the public domain no one permits him to leave his vessel there, whereas in the seller's domain the Gemara is uncertain because perhaps the seller lends him the place so he can acquire, since the seller wants the sale. Tur, siman 200, cites Ramah that the case of the buyer's vessel in the seller's domain concerns a seller who permitted the buyer to place the vessel there. Since he did not explicitly say, 'Go and acquire,' it remains uncertain whether the permission was intended to support acquisition. Likewise, the case of a seller's vessel in the buyer's domain concerns a seller who brought his vessel into the buyer's property with the buyer's permission. The Gemara is uncertain whether the seller's vessel remains sufficiently independent to interrupt the buyer's domain or becomes subordinate to the domain.

Here, by contrast, the trap was spread without the field owner's permission. It is not treated as a legally recognized vessel capable of interrupting the field owner's domain. The owner of the field therefore acquires. Maggid Mishneh's a fortiori argument is actually twofold: a buyer's vessel fails even though it was placed with permission and even though another person is consciously transferring ownership. All the more so should a trap spread without permission, where the trap does not count as an interrupting vessel at all and there is no conscious transferor, fail to acquire for the trap owner. But the field owner can acquire, because an unauthorized trap does not interrupt his domain. This is clear.

ולפי מ"ש ניחא כיון דקושיות רבא אינו אלא משום דס"ל ט"ה ממון וכמ"ש ומש"ה רב פפא שפיר משני דעת אחרת מקנה שאני דהא אגב וחליפין חשיבי קנינים גרועים ואינם נתפשים בטובת הנאה אבל חצר דהוא קנין טוב שפיר נקנה להם בתורת חצר דעת אחרת מקנה כיון דטובת הנאה ממון. ולכן נראה דהרי"ף והרמב"ם לטעמייהו במה דלא ס"ל הא דרב פפא וכן דעת הש"ע בסי' ר' אלא אפי' בדעת אחרת בעינן עומד בצדו דהא ליכא למימר טעמא דר"ג וזקנים משום דעת אחרת מקנה וכדרב פפא כיון דס"ל ט"ה אינה ממון אם כן ליכא דעת אחרת כלל וכמו שהקשה במרדכי אבל הרא"ש דפסק כדר' פפא שם בפ"א דמציעא משום דאזל לטעמיה שכת' דטובת הנאה ממון כמבואר ברא"ש פרק האיש מקדש דס"ל כר' חננאל דט"ה ממון א"כ שפיר אתיא כדרב פפא משום דקונה בתורת חצר שהוא קנין טוב:

אמנם אכתי איכא למידק כיון דהתם בעובדא דר"ג וזקנים הי' שנת הביעור דצריך להוציא מתחת ידו המתנות לכהן וללוי ולעני כמ"ש תו' שם בעובדא דר"ג וזקנים. וכיון דאפי' למ"ד טובת הנאה ממון אינו אלא בערך טובת הנאה הוא דאית להו לבעלים חלק וכמ"ש תוס' פ"ק דמציעא דף ז' בהא דאמרו שם תקפו כהן אין מוציאין אותו מידו והקשה אמאי אין מוציאין יאמרו הבעלים ליתן לכהן אחר ותירצו דאינו יכול לתובעו רק טובת הנאה שיש לו בו למ"ד ט"ה ממון עכ"ל ואם כן אכתי תיקשי נהי דט"ה ממון אכתי היכי מצי זכי בתורת חצר ובדעת אחרת מקנה לרב פפא נהי דזכה בערך טובת הנא' ע"י דעת אחרת מקנ' אבל גוף המתנות היכי מצי זכי כיון דאין להם לבעלים כלום בגוף המתנות וליכא דעת אחרת בגוף התבוא':

והנה לדעת הריטב"א ס"פ האיש מקדש דכת' בגונב תרומ' למ"ד ט"ה ממון הוי כל התרומ' שלו וצריך הגנב לשלם כפל כפי ערך כל התרומ' ע"ש א"כ ניחא לרב פפא משום דט"ה ממון הוי כל התבוא' של ר' גמליאל ע"י טובת הנא' ממון ושפיר נקנ' להם ע"י חצר ובדעת אחרת מקנ' אבל לפי מה שמבואר מדברי תוס' פ"ק דמציעא דאפי' למ"ד טובת הנא' ממון אינו אלא בערך ט"ה אם כן קשיא היכי זכו בגוף התבוא' ע"י חצר ודעת אחרת וכמ"ש. ולדברי ריטב"א יתעורר קושיות תוס' פ"ק דמציעא בהא דתקפו כהן אין מוציאין יאמרו הבעלים ליתן לכהן אחר וצ"ע. ולכן נרא' דלתירוצא דר' פפא הוי זכיית רבי יושיע ור"ע בתורת חצר וגם בתורת אגב דהיינו גוף התבוא' כיון דלית להו בעלים זכו בתורת אגב כמו שאר דבר הפקר ובערך ט"ה דהוי ממון ויש לו בעלים וקנין אגב אינו נתפס בו משום דה"ל קנין גרוע נקנ' בתורת חצר ודעת אחרת מקנ' כיון דבערך טובת הנא' ממון יש לו בעלים שפיר מהני בהו חצר ודעת אחרת מקנ'. ובזה ניחא ליישב מה דהקש' בש"ך בסי' ר' לדעת הרא"ש דפסק כר' פפא דחצר ודעת אחרת הי' הקנין א"כ הא דבעיא בש"ס פ"ק דקידושין דף כ"ו שדה במכר ומטלטלין במתנ' ופשוט לה מעובדא דר"ג וזקנים דהא לר' פפא ה"ל בתורת חצר ואם כן היכי פשיט מיניה קנין אגב. ולפמ"ש דלר' פפא נמי צריך קנין אגב דע"י חצר ודעת אחרת לא הי' נקנ' להם גוף התבוא' אלא בערך ט"ה שהוא ממון לבעלים ואינו נקנ' גוף התבוא' אלא בתורת אגב א"כ שפיר פשיט מינה קנין אגב והא דבעי למיפשט שם דבעי צבורין מדהקנ' להם מקומו דוקא. ולפי מ"ש בהפקר ודאי בעי צבורין אין זה קושיא דכבר דחו לה שם בטעם אחר שאמרו כי היכי דלא לטרחינהו אלא הא דפשיט שכירות בקרקע קשיא ולפמ"ש ניחא דגם לר' פפא צ"ל קנין אגב. ובזה נכון שיטת הרי"ף והרמב"ם ובעל העיטור ושטת הרא"ש הכל מיושב כהוגן ותן לחכם וגו':

וכאשר כתבתי הדברים לגדול אחד השיב וז"ל ונ"ל ראי' ברור' מש"ס פ"ק דקידושין דף כ"ז דבעי שדה לא' ומטלטלין לאחד מאי ואמאי לא בעי בש"ס איפכא שאם קנה קרקע אצל א' ומטלטלין אצל אחד ואמר הקונ' שיקנ' המטלטלין אלו אג"ק של זה אלא ודאי דלא אזלינן כלל בתר דעת הקונ' רק בתר דעת המקנ' א"כ בהפקר לא קנה המטלטלין אג"ק ועוד ראי' מתוס' פ' אלו מציאות (בבא מציעא דף כ"ו) ד"ה בדשתיק וא"ת וליקנ' ליה חצירו לבעל הגל ע"ש ואמאי לא הקש' דליקני ליה לבעל הגל בתורת אגב אלא ודאי לא שייך אגב בהפקר וגם תירוצם לא הוי שייך על קושיות אגב עכ"ל. אין זו השג' דמ"ש דאמאי דלא בעי בקנ' קרקע אצל א' ומטלטלין אצל אחר ודאי מודינא בשני בני אדם דהבעלים מחלקין דהא בקונ' מאדם אחד וליכא מצר מפסיק קנה בחזקה אחת כולה ואילו קנה משני בני אדם אע"ג דליכא מצר מפסיק צריך חזק' לכל א' וא' דרשות המוכרין מחלקן. וכיון דטעמא דקונ' הפקר בתורת אגב כל שצבורין בתוכו היינו משום דה"ל כמו גוף הקרקע ובשני בני אדם אפי' הן מחוברין רשות המוכרין מפסקת ביניהם:

ומה שהביא ראי' מדברי ר"י פ' א"מ במה דלא הקשו מתורת אגב אינ' ראי' כלל דודאי כל הקנינים משיכ' ומסיר' וחזק' צריך דעת לקנין אלא חצירו של אדם הוא דזוכ' שלא מדעתו ומש"ה לא קשיא להו דליקני בתורת חצר דקונ' שלא מדעת אבל אגב צריך דעת לקנין ועיין שו"ת מוהרי"ט ח"א סי' ק"נ וז"ל מיהו י"ל דידו עדיף מעודר דאשכחן חצירו של אדם קונ' שלא מדעתו כו' וכיון דחצירו קונ' שלא מדעתו כ"ש ידו וכו' ועודר שאני דמדין חזק' היא ולא מתורת זכי' ע"ש. וא"כ אגב הרי הוא כמו כל הקנינים דצריך דעת ועמ"ש בסי' רס"א סק"ב:

ושוב מצאתי להדיא בחידושי הרשב"א כדברינו דהפקר נמי נקנ' בתורת אגב ע"ש פ' הפר' דף נ"ב וז"ל ושטרא נמי לא קנה דלאו אדעתא דשטרא מחזיק כלומר וכל שהחזיק בקרקע יכול להוציא השטר מידו דהמחזיק בקרקע קנה השטר בכל מקום שהוא דשטרא אפסרא דארעא עכ"ל. וזה שהחזיק בקרקע דקונ' השטר בכל מקום שהוא אינו אלא בתורת אגב וכמבואר בפ' הספינ' דף פ"ו בהא דתני שם שלש' שטרות כו' ע"ש והתם פ' הפר' מיירי בנכסי הגר א"כ מוכח דקונ' אג"ק בהפקר ואע"ג דכתבנו דהפקר בעי צבורין היינו משום דשטרא אפסרא דארעא ה"ל כמו קרקע ואינו צ"ל קני השטר אג"ק וזה ברור:
en_segments: Once he struck it with one blow of a hoe, he acquires the whole. I was uncertain whether one who takes possession of ownerless property of a deceased convert and movable property is located within it acquires the movables through agav. Perhaps acquisition by agav works only where another person consciously transfers ownership, while one who acquires on his own cannot use agav. The practical difference arises where courtyard acquisition is unavailable, such as an unguarded area where the acquirer does not stand nearby and did not say, 'My field shall acquire for me.'

At first glance there is proof from houses acquired by chazakah in the estate of a convert, as indicated in Bava Batra 33 concerning two houses, one inside the other. According to authorities who treat a house as an item detached and then affixed, with the law of movable property as explained in siman 95, and according to what I wrote there in seif katan 3 citing Magen Avraham, siman 637, such a house must be acquired through agav. This would prove that ownerless property can be acquired through agav. Yet one can answer that the house is acquired through courtyard acquisition once the person acquires the ground beneath it, in accordance with what I wrote in siman 202 that acquisition of the courtyard and of the gift can arrive simultaneously.

There is, however, a clear proof that ownerless property can be acquired by agav from Bava Kamma 117. Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages dispute whether one who stole land that was then swept away by a river must replace it, depending on whether land can be stolen. Rav Pappa explains the baraita about one who stole a cow that was swept away by a river as a case where he stole a field containing a cow lying in it. Rabbi Eliezer follows his view that land can be stolen, while the Sages follow theirs. Rashi explains that the robber did not physically pull the cow. According to Rabbi Eliezer, because the field is acquired to the robber for purposes of liability, the cow lying in it is acquired together with the field through agav, and the robber must pay. According to the Sages, he acquires neither the field nor the cow. In a robber's case there is no conscious transferor. The robber nevertheless needs an acquisition to become liable for accidents just as a purchaser needs an acquisition to acquire. Rashi says he acquires the cow through agav. This proves that agav works even in self-acquisition from ownerless-like property.

Rashi did not explain that the cow was acquired through the courtyard, even though the robber acquires the field for purposes of liability, because courtyard acquisition depends on a person's legal domain. A robber acquires the land only for liability for unavoidable loss and has no legitimate proprietary domain in it. Although in cases of property susceptible to theft the robber pays according to the time of theft and need not pay for use, as explained in simanim 363 and 371, that does not make the unlawfully occupied courtyard his domain. He entered without permission. Hence Rashi correctly uses agav rather than courtyard acquisition.

There is nevertheless an important distinction between ownerless property and a gift. For a gift, we rule that movables need not be physically gathered upon the land for agav acquisition, as stated in siman 202. For ownerless property they certainly must be gathered there. If one acquired the estate of a convert, he clearly cannot say that by agav he intends to acquire every ownerless object in the world. The reason is that ordinary agav without physical presence requires the transferor to say, 'Acquire it together with the land.' With ownerless property there is no transferor who can say this. Even if the acquirer himself says, 'I wish to acquire it through agav,' that cannot substitute for another person's instruction. But where the movables are physically gathered upon the land, Rambam, chapter 22 of Hilchot Mechirah, holds that no statement of 'acquire through agav' is necessary. Maggid Mishneh explains that the Gemara's rule that agav does not require the movables to be gathered applies where the transferor expressly says, 'Acquire them together with the land,' whereas without that formula the movables must be physically there. When the movables are gathered upon the land they are treated as part of the land itself. Therefore self-acquisition from ownerless property works in that form as well. This also explains why Bava Kamma specifically says the cow was lying within the field. If agav never required physical presence, that detail would be unnecessary. But because no transferor exists to say, 'Acquire through agav,' the cow must be gathered there. This is strong proof for Rambam's distinction between agav with and without physical presence, despite Maggid Mishneh, Ran, and Rosh questioning Rambam's rule that gathered movables do not require an express agav formula.

A difficulty arises from Bava Metzia 11. The Gemara requires a person to stand next to his field for courtyard acquisition. Rabbi Abba challenges Ulla from Rabban Gamliel's tithe distribution, where Rabban Gamliel said, 'The tithe that I will measure is given to Yehoshua, and its place is rented to him,' and similarly concerning Rabbi Akiva. They were not standing beside Rabban Gamliel's field. Ulla answered sharply that the transaction there was through agav. Rabbi Zeira accepted this, but Rabbi Abba did not. Rava said Rabbi Abba was correct not to accept it: did they have no sudar with which to acquire by chalipin? Rather, the benefit of choosing the recipient of tithes is not monetary property that can be acquired by chalipin, and similarly is not monetary property that can be acquired through agav. Rashi explains that the entitlement was not Rabban Gamliel's property. He merely rendered it ownerless toward the recipients, and by renting them its location the courtyard acquired it for them like other hefker.

According to what I have written, if hefker can be acquired through agav when physically gathered upon the land, why does Rava compare agav to chalipin? Chalipin certainly fails because the right of choosing the recipient is not money and therefore is not the owner's transferable property. But agav could still work through the recipients' self-acquisition of the hefker, just as a courtyard can acquire hefker.

This can be answered from Shitah Mekubetzet there. It writes that even if one holds that the benefit of choosing the recipient is monetary, it is not sufficiently substantial money to be acquired by chalipin. The sugya can therefore fit both the view that it is not money and the view that it is money. Although it cannot be acquired by chalipin or agav because those are relatively weak modes of acquisition, if one gave a person a maneh and transferred his entitlement in the produce, the recipient could acquire it. Otherwise the Gemara would have said simply that the entitlement is not money and cannot be acquired at all. The formulation, 'not money to acquire by chalipin,' implies that there are modes through which it can be acquired. This is necessary because Rava explicitly holds in Nedarim 85 that the right of choosing the recipient is money. Rava therefore means: even if it is money, it is too slight a proprietary interest for the weaker kinyanim of chalipin and agav.

Accordingly, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva could not acquire the property on their own as hefker according to Rava, because Rava holds that Rabban Gamliel retained a monetary proprietary interest in the selection right. The property therefore still had an owner. Rabban Gamliel, however, could not transfer that slight proprietary interest through the weaker acquisitions of chalipin or agav. This also reconciles Rif's position. Rif requires standing beside one's field even when another person consciously transfers ownership, rejecting Rav Pappa's distinction that a conscious transferor is different. Commentators asked: if so, how can the Rabban Gamliel episode be explained through agav, when we rule that the choice benefit is not money and the owner cannot transfer it, while courtyard acquisition should fail because the recipients were not beside the field? According to what I wrote, Rif and Rambam hold that the benefit of choosing the recipient is not money at all. It is therefore ownerless with respect to the recipients, who can acquire it themselves through agav when the produce is gathered on the rented land. Rava himself, who holds that the benefit is money, cannot use that explanation, because the property still belongs to Rabban Gamliel and the slight proprietary interest cannot be transferred by weak modes of acquisition.

The same resolves Baal HaItur's view. Shach in siman 203 challenges Rama's ruling, from Hagahot Maimoniyot in the name of Baal HaItur, that the choice benefit cannot be acquired through chalipin. Baal HaItur elsewhere writes that mere rental of the place would not have acquired in the Rabban Gamliel case without agav. Thus he evidently explains that episode as agav. How then can he say the choice benefit is not acquired by chalipin but is acquired by agav? According to what I wrote, Baal HaItur can hold that the choice benefit is not money and cannot be transferred by the owner at all. Rama similarly rules in siman 276 that it cannot even be inherited. But when the produce itself is physically in the recipients' possession, they can acquire it on their own through agav as ownerless property. Shach himself distinguishes that although the owner cannot transfer a nonproprietary choice right when it is in another person's hands, a person may obtain it when it is physically in his own control.

Mordechai in the first chapter of Bava Metzia asks against Rav Pappa's answer, 'a conscious transferor is different': if the choice benefit is not money, there is no conscious transferor at all and the recipients should be acquiring on their own. Mordechai answers that because Rabban Gamliel transferred the courtyard to them as well, with respect to the courtyard there was a conscious transferor. According to what I wrote, Rav Pappa's answer works particularly well if, like Rava, he holds the choice benefit is money. Agav and chalipin are weak and cannot transfer that slight interest, but courtyard acquisition is a stronger kinyan and can work through a conscious transferor. Therefore, if the right is monetary, Rabban Gamliel's conscious transfer through the rented courtyard is effective. Rif and Rambam, who hold the right is not money, cannot explain the episode that way and accordingly reject Rav Pappa's distinction, requiring the recipient to stand beside the courtyard even when there is a conscious transferor. Rosh, who rules like Rav Pappa, follows his own view in chapter HaIsh Mekadesh that the choice benefit is money, in accordance with Rabbeinu Chananel. Thus all the approaches fit their broader positions.

There remains another difficulty. The Rabban Gamliel episode occurred in the year of removal, when he had to remove the priestly, Levite, and poor tithes from his possession. Even according to the view that the choice benefit is money, the owner has only the economic value of that choice, not ownership of the entire produce. Tosafos in Bava Metzia 7, regarding a Kohen who seizes a doubtful firstborn animal, explain that even according to the view that the owner's choice right is money, the owner can claim only the value of his choice, not the whole gift. If so, how could Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva acquire the body of the produce through a courtyard and conscious transferor under Rav Pappa? Rabban Gamliel had conscious transferable ownership only in the value of the choice right, not in the body of the gifts.

Ritva at the end of HaIsh Mekadesh writes that according to the view that the choice benefit is money, a thief who steals terumah must pay double according to the full value of the terumah, because the entire terumah is considered the owner's property through the monetary value of his choice. According to Ritva, Rav Pappa's explanation is straightforward: if the choice right is money, all the produce is treated as Rabban Gamliel's and can be transferred through courtyard acquisition with a conscious transferor. Yet this creates a difficulty with Tosafos in Bava Metzia 7, who hold that even according to the view that choice benefit is money the owner can claim only its limited value.

It therefore appears that according to Rav Pappa the acquisition in Rabban Gamliel's episode operated through both courtyard and agav. The body of the produce, insofar as it had no owner, was acquired through agav like other hefker, because it was physically gathered on the transferred ground. The monetary value of the choice right, which belonged to Rabban Gamliel and cannot be acquired through the weak kinyan of agav, was acquired through the courtyard with a conscious transferor, which is a strong acquisition. This also resolves Shach's question in siman 200 against Rosh. Rosh rules like Rav Pappa that the Rabban Gamliel episode worked through courtyard acquisition with a conscious transferor. Yet Kiddushin 26 asks whether land in a sale can carry movable property given as a gift through agav and resolves it from the Rabban Gamliel episode. If Rav Pappa explains the episode only through courtyard acquisition, how can it prove agav? According to what I wrote, even Rav Pappa must use agav for the body of the produce. The courtyard acquisition with a conscious transferor transfers only the monetary value of the owner's choice right. Thus the episode remains a proof for agav. As for the Gemara's attempt to prove that the movables must be physically gathered there from Rabban Gamliel's renting their exact location, our approach indeed requires physical presence for hefker. But the Gemara rejects that proof on another ground, namely that the exact location was rented merely to spare the recipients inconvenience. The remaining agav proof is still valid.

After I wrote this, a distinguished scholar responded that there is a clear proof against me from Kiddushin 27, which asks whether land can be given to one person and movables to another through agav. Why does it not ask the reverse, where one acquires land from one owner and movables from another and the acquirer says he wishes to acquire the movables through agav of the first owner's land? This shows, he argued, that agav depends entirely on the transferor's intent, and therefore cannot acquire hefker. He further cited Tosafos, Bava Metzia 26, s.v. 'where he remained silent,' who ask why a courtyard should not acquire a found object for the owner of a heap. Why did they not ask that he acquire it through agav? Their answer concerning courtyard acquisition would not address agav.

This is not a refutation. Regarding land and movables owned by two different people, I agree that the distinct owners divide the acquisitions. Where one buys adjoining fields from one person, one act of chazakah can acquire all when no boundary separates them, whereas fields bought from two different owners require a separate chazakah for each even without a physical boundary, because the distinct ownerships divide them. My claim about hefker is only that where movables are physically gathered on the land, they are treated as part of the land itself. With two owners, the distinct ownerships prevent that unity. As for Tosafos in Bava Metzia 26, ordinary modes of acquisition such as meshichah, mesirah, chazakah, and agav require intent to acquire. A person's courtyard is exceptional in that it acquires without his knowledge. Hence Tosafos ask only about the courtyard, which could acquire automatically. Agav would require the owner's intent, and therefore their failure to ask about agav proves nothing. Maharit, part 1 siman 150, likewise distinguishes the hand and courtyard, which acquire without awareness, from ordinary chazakah. See what I wrote in siman 261, seif katan 2.

I later found Rashba's novellae explicitly supporting my position that hefker can be acquired through agav. In Bava Kamma 52 he writes that where one took possession of the land but not the document, the document is nonetheless acquired wherever it is, because the document is the tether of the land. A document attached to land in this way is acquired through agav, as is clear from Bava Batra 86 concerning the three types of documents. The Bava Kamma passage concerns the estate of a deceased convert. Thus Rashba explicitly recognizes agav acquisition in hefker. en_segments: To travel by a specified route. At the beginning of chapter HaShoel the baraita derives the borrower's liability for theft and loss by an a fortiori argument from a paid bailee. One might ask that the argument can be refuted because a paid bailee can become liable for double payment when he falsely claims an armed robber took the deposit. Yet the Gemara says that certain principal payment without an oath is more severe than the possibility of double payment that depends upon an oath. What, however, is the proposed refutation? A borrower too can sometimes become liable for double payment if he falsely claims that an armed robber took the object on the specified road for which it was borrowed, since an armed robber has the status of a thief. Nevertheless, because double payment is far more common with a paid bailee, whereas with a borrower it occurs only where he borrowed the object for travel on a specified road, this can still be regarded as a relevant distinction. See Tosafos at the end of chapter HaMafkid. This also resolves the textual reading at the beginning of Bava Kamma, 4b. The Gemara asks why Rabbi Oshaya does not list thief and robber separately, including double, fourfold, and fivefold payments, and answers that he already listed them through the unpaid bailee and borrower. Rashi explains that an unpaid bailee can encompass both a thief and robber: if he falsely claims theft he becomes like a thief, and if he falsely claims robbery he becomes like a robber. Rashi rejects the reading 'borrower,' because a borrower cannot exempt himself through a claim of theft. Tosafos write similarly. According to what I have written, however, a borrower can indeed encompass thief and robber where he borrowed the object for a specified route. If he claims that an armed robber attacked him on that route, it is a claim of theft; if he claims ordinary robbers attacked him, it is a claim of robbery. In such circumstances those claims exempt him because the loss occurred through the use for which it was borrowed.

He did not notice immediately. This ruling is from the Rosh: since the borrower does not know whether the animal died because of its work or for another reason, he must pay. Beit Yosef asks why he should be obligated because of a doubt and therefore omitted this ruling from Shulchan Aruch. The Shach answers that the borrower is one who is obligated to swear but cannot swear, because he cannot take a definite oath, and Terumat HaDeshen, siman 333, similarly writes that a bailee who says, 'I do not know whether the loss resulted from negligence,' is obligated to pay because he is obligated to swear but cannot swear. Nimukei Yosef, however, does not appear to hold this way. At the end of Bava Kamma he discusses when a bailee's obligation begins, at meshichah or at negligence, and cites Ramah: the practical difference is a borrower who borrows a donkey for his agent to ride and it dies on the road, and he does not know whether it died because of the work. Since he does not become obligated until the time of the accident, he is exempt, because his claim is 'I do not know whether I ever became obligated.' But if he borrowed a donkey for himself to ride and then gave it to his agent, and there is a doubt whether it died because of the work, he is liable, because a borrower has no right to lend the animal to another. His liability therefore began at the time of that negligence, making his claim analogous to 'I do not know whether I repaid you,' which is liable. This shows that Ramah does not apply the rule that a bailee who says 'I do not know' is automatically one obligated to swear who cannot swear. Otherwise even one who borrowed it for his agent to ride would be liable through that rule. Beit Yosef, siman 291, cites the students of Rashba regarding a paid bailee who entrusted the object to his wife, children, or someone to whom the owner regularly entrusts property. Ramban holds that if the second bailee, who is unpaid, swears that he was not negligent and claims it was stolen or lost, the first bailee remains liable; he cannot say perhaps it died through an unavoidable accident and I am exempt, because it is upon him to establish his exemption. The same applies if the second bailee refuses to swear or traveled overseas. Rabbi Yom Tov ben Rabbi Shmuel agrees. Another opinion, however, holds that if the paid bailee delivered the property to an unpaid bailee and the second refuses to swear, the first is exempt, even if the owner makes a definite claim, because the first says he does not know and his case is like one who is told, 'You owe me a maneh,' and answers, 'I do not know whether I became obligated.' The Shach in siman 291 discusses this at length and asks against this latter view: we expressly rule that even an unpaid bailee who transfers property to a paid bailee is liable because the owner may say, 'You are believed by me with an oath; the other is not believed by me.' Thus even if the second wishes to swear, the first remains liable, all the more so if the second refuses to swear. The Shach concludes that a bailee who says 'I do not know' is like one who says, 'I do not know whether I returned it.' Once he became a bailee, his uncertainty is not whether he ever became obligated. Even according to those who hold that a bailee's property becomes encumbered only from the time of negligence, it is still treated as 'I do not know whether I returned it.' He proves this from Tosafos in chapter HaShoel, 97a, regarding the Mishnah of one who borrowed one cow and another was rented. Tosafos say that 'I do not know whether you lent to me' is exempt but 'I do not know whether I returned it' is liable. Although there the owner gave him two cows, once he returns one, the remaining uncertainty is like 'I do not know whether you ever lent me the other.' The Shach infers that if he did not return either one and simply said he did not know, the case would be 'I do not know whether I returned.' Yam Shel Shlomo in chapter HaGozel cites Nimukei Yosef and questions him similarly. He ultimately rules that even if the lender also says 'perhaps,' the borrower is liable because he cannot swear with certainty. Elsewhere Yam Shel Shlomo treats the case as 'I do not know whether I repaid,' requiring a definite claim by the lender even according to those who hold that a bailee becomes obligated only at negligence.

In my opinion, Ramah's position is correct from every angle. According to the view that a bailee becomes obligated only at negligence, while the object remains intact there is no monetary obligation at all. Yam Shel Shlomo's assertion that the bailee is obligated to return the animal is incorrect. A bailee has no independent mitzvah or monetary obligation of return while the object remains intact. A thief and robber are commanded to return what they took, but a bailee is not. The object remains in the owner's domain wherever it is, and the owner retrieves his own property. As I wrote in siman 86, seif katan 4, and siman 198, seif katan 8, only when the object was lost through negligence does the Torah say 'he shall bring a witness,' meaning that he must bring evidence before beit din concerning what happened. If it was lost through an unavoidable accident, there is no general duty of return, all the more so while the object remains intact. Even according to the version that a bailee becomes obligated from meshichah, Ritva treats the uncertainty as 'I do not know whether I ever became obligated,' cited in Shitah Mekubetzet to chapter HaShoel, 99a. Ritva explains that even according to the opinion that a borrower's liability begins at meshichah, this does not mean a complete immediate monetary liability. So long as the cow remains alive, it remains entirely in the owner's domain and the bailee owes nothing. Rather, if it is later stolen or suffers an accident, his property becomes retroactively encumbered from the time of meshichah, with practical consequences for property sold in the interim. Some Geonim erred on this point, as Ritva states. Thus while the object is intact there is no existing debt and not even an independent obligation of return upon a bailee.

This also answers Yam Shel Shlomo's second contention. Ramah holds that even according to the version that liability begins at the accident, once the borrower gives the animal to another person, that act is at least the beginning of negligence, because a borrower may not lend another's property. Although if it later dies through a true unavoidable accident the borrower may ultimately be exempt, since the transfer to another is not itself necessarily full negligence after the fact, it nevertheless begins a state of fault and creates potential liability. A later unavoidable accident then functions as a discharge from that potential liability, just as according to the version that liability begins with meshichah, an unavoidable accident can discharge the bailee. Thus if he borrowed it for himself and transferred it to his agent, the act of unauthorized transfer creates the initial liability, and when he later says he does not know whether the death was because of the work, he is saying, 'I do not know whether I was discharged.' By contrast, if he borrowed it from the outset for his agent to ride, there was no initial improper transfer and the uncertainty is whether liability ever arose. Ramban's words in Shitah Mekubetzet to Ketubot likewise show that when the father failed before death to instruct his heirs that the cow was borrowed property, this is treated as the negligence from which later liability developed. Nimukei Yosef's language similarly says that the heirs' liability after slaughter arises from the father's negligence, because from the time of negligence that causes the eventual accident, the bailee's liability begins. The same principle applies when a bailee transfers the object to one to whom he was not entitled to transfer it: that act is at least a partial negligence and brings potential liability into existence. A later unavoidable accident can then operate as a return or discharge.

This also explains the opinion among the students of Rashba that a first bailee who transfers the object to someone whom the owner regularly trusts is exempt if the second refuses to swear. The Shach asks that ordinarily a bailee who transfers to another bailee is liable even if the second is willing to swear, because the owner says, 'You are believed by me with an oath; the second is not.' But the ordinary transfer itself is an improper act and therefore creates initial liability. If later there is uncertainty whether the ultimate loss was unavoidable, it is like 'I do not know whether I was discharged.' When, however, the object was transferred to someone whom the owner regularly uses and to whom the first bailee was permitted to transfer it initially, there is no negligence at all in the transfer. The first bailee's uncertainty is therefore whether any liability ever arose, and he is exempt even if the second refuses to swear. This is precisely analogous to Ramah's borrower who borrowed the donkey specifically for his agent to ride.

The same reasoning explains the ruling concerning a shepherd who leaves his flock and we assess whether he could have saved it. If it is not known whether he could have saved it, he is liable. The shepherd was at least somewhat negligent in leaving the flock, so initial potential liability arose. The later uncertainty whether the ultimate event was unavoidable is then an uncertainty whether he was discharged. Moreover, where an event begins with negligence and the eventual loss could have come from that negligence, he is liable unless it is clearly established that the unavoidable accident was unrelated. This is the principle of an event that began with negligence, as in the case of the willow hut. Thus the shepherd remains liable unless it is affirmatively shown that the loss was not caused by the negligence.

Yam Shel Shlomo further argues that if the lender himself also says 'perhaps,' both parties are uncertain and the borrower should be exempt even under the rule of 'I do not know whether I repaid.' Ramah can hold, however, that only in an ordinary loan, where the lender should know whether he was repaid, does the lender's uncertainty defeat recovery. Where the claimant had no reason to know the event, even a claimant who says 'perhaps' can recover from a defendant whose uncertainty is one of repayment, as discussed by Mishneh LaMelech and cited in siman 75. The Shach's proof from Tosafos in chapter HaShoel is also not decisive. Tosafos expressly continue that even with one cow, when he does not know whether it died while borrowed, the case is like 'I do not know whether you lent it to me.' Tosafos therefore explicitly treat even one animal in this way, consistent either with the view that a bailee becomes liable only from negligence or with Ritva's explanation that even under the meshichah view the earlier obligation is only conditional.

One point nevertheless still requires explanation in Ramah. Even if under his analysis the borrower who borrowed for his agent says 'I do not know whether I ever became obligated,' why is he not liable as one obligated to swear who cannot swear, as Terumat HaDeshen rules regarding a bailee who does not know whether the loss was negligent? It appears that Ramah holds that the essential oath of bailees is the oath that the object is no longer in his possession, as Maggid Mishneh writes in chapter 4 of Hilchot She'eilah and as ruled in siman 294. If the borrower recognizes the dead animal and the only uncertainty is whether the death resulted from negligence or from the work, that issue is only a matter added through gilgul. He therefore holds that the rule 'one who is obligated to swear and cannot swear must pay' does not apply to a matter added only through gilgul. Certainly, where the principal oath itself is imposed on the basis of uncertainty, one does not create liability through inability to answer the gilgul. Beit Yosef's difficulty against the Rosh can be understood similarly. The Rosh, by contrast, follows his view that the oath 'I was not negligent' is itself one of the primary oaths of bailees, and therefore if the bailee cannot swear it with certainty he is one obligated to swear who cannot swear and must pay. There is also an additional reason not to impose payment merely because the bailee says 'I do not know.' Rashi in chapter HaShoel, 98a, explains that according to Rami bar Chama, the four bailees require not merely an admission but an additional denial, such as 'it never happened' or 'I returned it.' According to Rashi, 'I do not know' is not itself a denial. The rule of partial admission with 'fifty I know and fifty I do not know' creates liability because the admission obligates an oath on the remainder, and the uncertainty then makes him unable to swear. Likewise, with one witness, the witness itself creates the oath. But the special oath of bailees, where there is no independent admission, may not arise at all when the bailee says only 'I do not know,' since uncertainty is not a denial. Tosafos disagree and treat 'I do not know' as a denial, which would make the rule of inability to swear more broadly applicable. Beit Yosef may follow Rashi's approach and therefore refuse to impose payment merely because of the doubt.

See also Rif and Rambam, chapter 3 of Hilchot Sechirut, regarding an armed shepherd confronted by armed robbers, where the unresolved Talmudic question is ruled leniently. At first glance this is difficult according to Terumat HaDeshen, because every bailee must swear definitively that he was exempt, and here the legal status itself is doubtful. The answer is that even Terumat HaDeshen speaks only of factual uncertainty, where the bailee cannot say what actually happened, whether negligence or an unavoidable accident. But where the facts are fully known and only the legal classification is doubtful, he can swear to the facts with certainty, and because of the legal doubt we do not extract money. One might still object based on Maharanach's position that where the uncertainty concerns only a possible discharge from an otherwise existing debt, one cannot plead 'kim li' and the case is like 'I do not know whether I repaid.' However, Kesef Mishneh writes that according to his version of the Gemara the question concerning an armed shepherd against armed robbers was actually resolved in favor of exemption. The difficulty therefore falls away.
